name: Median rhomboid glossitis
aliases: central papillary atrophy of the tongue

clinicalPearls: A well-demarcated rhomboid or oval area of papillary atrophy in the midline of the tongue dorsum, just anterior to the circumvallate papillae
It is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, appearing smooth, red and depapillated
There is a strong association with Candida colonisation, and it is often regarded as a form of chronic mucosal candidosis
Smoking, denture use, inhaled corticosteroids and immunosuppression are recognised associations
A matching (kissing) lesion on the opposing palate suggests more extensive candidal involvement
Management includes antifungal therapy where Candida is implicated and addressing predisposing factors
reference.pathophysiology: Median rhomboid glossitis is a localised area of atrophy of the filiform papillae in the midline dorsal tongue. Although historically attributed to a developmental defect, it is now strongly linked to chronic Candida colonisation of the site, with the yeast contributing to the persistent papillary atrophy. Local factors that favour candidal overgrowth, such as smoking, corticosteroid inhalers and immunosuppression, promote the lesion, and the condition is considered a chronic candidal-associated process rather than a primary invasive infection.
additionalDifferentials: Erythematous candidosis elsewhere on the tongue
Squamous cell carcinoma or other tongue neoplasm (if indurated)
Lingual thyroid or other midline swelling
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic midline site and appearance
Mycological assessment for Candida where indicated
Review of predisposing factors (smoking, inhaled steroids, immune status)
Biopsy if there is induration, ulceration or diagnostic doubt
redFlags: Induration, ulceration or a mass suggesting malignancy
Failure to respond to antifungal treatment
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign; it often improves with antifungal treatment and control of predisposing factors, though the depapillated area may persist.
pitfalls: Mistaking an indurated lesion for the benign condition and missing carcinoma
Overlooking the candidal association and predisposing factors
Failing to examine the opposing palate for a kissing lesion
management: Topical antifungal therapy with an azole such as miconazole gel or with nystatin where Candida is implicated
Systemic azole antifungal such as fluconazole for extensive, symptomatic or refractory candidal involvement, including a kissing palatal lesion
Smoking cessation as a key modifiable predisposing factor
Optimise inhaler technique with mouth-rinsing after inhaled corticosteroids and attend to denture hygiene
Address underlying immunosuppression and glycaemic control where relevant
Reassure that the lesion is benign, though the depapillated area may persist
Biopsy if there is induration, ulceration or diagnostic uncertainty to exclude other pathology

Enlarged tongue; may be part of a syndrome in developmental conditions such as Down syndrome, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; may be due to tumor (hemangioma or lymphangioma), metabolic disease (such as primary amyloidosis), or endocrine disturbance (such as acromegaly or cretinism).
Dorsal surface and sides covered by painless shallow or deep fissures that may collect debris and become irritated.

rows.parameter: Median rhomboid glossitis (size or morphology change)

cells.text: Congenital abnormality with an ovoid, denuded area in the median posterior tongue; may be associated with candidiasis and may respond to antifungals.

rows.parameter: Geographic tongue, benign migratory glossitis (color change)

cells.text: Asymptomatic inflammatory condition with rapid loss and regrowth of filiform papillae, giving denuded red patches that wander across the tongue surface.

Elongated filiform papillae of the medial dorsal surface because the keratin layer fails to desquamate normally; brownish-black color may come from staining by tobacco, food, or chromogenic organisms.
Appearance in scarlet fever from hypertrophy of fungiform papillae plus changes in filiform papillae.

Atrophy that may be associated with xerostomia, pernicious anemia, iron-deficiency anemia, pellagra, or syphilis; may cause painful burning; may reflect erythematous candidiasis and respond to antifungals.
